video_title: He Did Everything Right and Still Lost His Bitcoin | Jonathan Goodman on the Coldcard Hack
gist: Jonathan Goodman, author and Cold Card hardware-wallet user, lost 18+ Bitcoin (~$1M+, later cited near $1.6M) to a firmware entropy flaw in Cold Card devices made by Coin Kite (NVK), despite using five layers of self-custody best practice (trusted vendor, device-aged transactions, safety-deposit-box storage, metal seed backup, and splitting funds across three devices) because every layer relied on the same flawed key-generation process — a textbook 'common cause failure.' The episode is a case study in why redundancy without diversifying the underlying failure domain is an illusion, plus a sober look at the economics of post-hack legal recourse and why the guest's Bitcoin thesis and asymmetric-bet position-sizing philosophy survived the loss intact.

themes.theme: Cold Card Hack Mechanics & Root Cause

insights.claim: The Cold Card hack stemmed from a firmware flaw in which seed-phrase entropy generation was not done properly, making seed phrases guessable/brute-forceable rather than requiring any compromise of the physical device or user error.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Goodman
insights.so_what: A hardware-wallet vendor's key-generation implementation, not just its physical security model, is a critical and hard-to-verify risk surface for any self-custody product.
insights.quote: the entropy of the seed phrase was not done properly

insights.claim: The flawed entropy appears to have affected devices only up to a certain point in time, with devices manufactured after that point seemingly unaffected, which the guest argues suggests Coin Kite itself was likely unaware of the defect rather than knowingly sitting on it.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Goodman
insights.so_what: Distinguishes an undiscovered defect from a cover-up, which matters for assessing vendor liability and whether other 'quietly patched' vulnerabilities may exist industry-wide.
insights.quote: if that were true, then the newer devices would have all had fixed entropy

insights.claim: The guest believes an AI system was likely used to scan many codebases at once to search for exploitable backdoors, rather than the attack being a targeted effort specifically against Coin Kite.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Goodman
insights.so_what: AI-assisted vulnerability discovery across many codebases at once raises the baseline threat level for every hardware/software vendor, not just the one that gets hit first.
insights.quote: Here's a whole whack of code bases. Find me something.

insights.claim: The Cold Card hack unfolded in successive waves of exploitation, with the first wave (which hit the guest) reportedly the least sophisticated, and later waves becoming more sophisticated as more attackers learned of and exploited the same backdoor.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Goodman
insights.so_what: Once a critical vulnerability becomes public, exploitation accelerates and diversifies quickly — incident response speed matters more than initial containment alone.

insights.claim: There is speculation, unconfirmed, that attackers may have used on-chain analysis to identify and drain the largest-balance wallets first, anticipating that news of the hack would spread fast and other opportunistic hackers would pile on afterward.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Goodman
insights.so_what: Large self-custody balances that are in any way identifiable on-chain may be preferentially targeted first once a systemic vulnerability surfaces, favoring speed of remediation for the biggest holders.

themes.theme: Common Cause Failure: The Central Security Lesson

insights.claim: Despite using five separate layers of protection (buying the vendor widely considered most secure, aging the device before transacting, storing devices in a bank safety-deposit box, metal-stamping a seed-phrase backup, and splitting funds across three separate devices), every layer failed simultaneously because all five relied on the same underlying flawed key-generation process — what engineers call a 'common cause failure.'
insights.speaker: Jonathan Goodman
insights.so_what: Redundancy only reduces risk if the redundant layers fail independently; stacking multiple protections from a single point of technical origin provides an illusion of safety, not actual diversification.
insights.quote: Every every piece of protection that I had was protecting against the same vulnerability.

insights.claim: The term for the failure mode is 'common cause failure': multiple safeguards that all trace back to one shared root cause (here, one company's entropy-generation code) fail together, so quantity of backups or storage locations does not equal true redundancy.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Goodman
insights.so_what: Investors and self-custodians should audit whether their 'diversified' backups actually diversify the underlying failure domain (e.g., different hardware vendors and different entropy sources), not just the number of physical copies.
insights.quote: Engineers call it common cause failure.

insights.claim: The guest generalizes common-cause-failure risk beyond Bitcoin: storing many complex, unique passwords in a single password manager, or connecting all home security devices to one shared Wi-Fi network, are structurally identical single points of failure that most people don't recognize as such.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Goodman
insights.so_what: A useful personal-risk checklist: identify every place in your digital/financial life where multiple 'independent' safeguards actually share one root dependency.
insights.quote: we all create all of these complicated passwords and then we store them all in the same password manager. We all have Ring devices and security systems for our house that are all connected to the same Wi-Fi.

insights.claim: Multisig setups appear to have protected many self-custody users from this specific hack in a way that splitting funds across multiple single-sig devices from the same vendor did not, because multisig does not depend on one company's entropy generation for the entire spendable key.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Goodman
insights.so_what: Multisig across genuinely independent hardware/software providers is a materially different risk profile than N single-sig devices from one vendor, even though both look like 'multiple device' redundancy on the surface.
insights.quote: I did multisig. That was I think for a lot of people that saved them the multisig aspect

insights.claim: The Bitcoin community mantra 'don't trust, verify' breaks down for the average holder because most people are not technically capable of independently verifying low-level firmware or entropy-generation code, and instead end up trusting other trusted parties (vendors, auditors, community reputation) on their behalf.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Goodman
insights.so_what: Self-custody's core promise of trustlessness is, in practice, layered trust for most users — a gap that vendor audits and third-party security research need to close rather than assume away.
insights.quote: Yes, we say don't trust verify. But there are some things that we can't verify. There's some things that I'm not technical enough to verify myself. So, I put trust in other people that I thought had verified.

insights.claim: Immediately upon discovering the theft, the guest's first priority was building a documented digital paper trail — filing a support ticket with Coin Kite and posting publicly on X — specifically anticipating that the company would later be subpoenaed and sued, even though he expected no direct help from the ticket itself.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Goodman
insights.so_what: In any large-scale digital-asset loss, immediate, deliberate evidence preservation (support tickets, timestamped public posts) materially strengthens a victim's position in future litigation or claims processes.

insights.claim: Filing a police report for a large crypto theft required physical presence at a local police station, and the responding non-emergency hotline operators and initial desk officers were largely unequipped to handle a six-figure-plus cybercrime report, though a dedicated cyber-crime detective was eventually engaged.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Goodman
insights.so_what: Victims of large crypto theft should expect friction and a knowledge gap at the first point of law-enforcement contact, and should escalate toward a cybercrime unit as quickly as possible rather than relying on general police response.

insights.claim: The investigating detective told the guest directly that law enforcement's job is to catch the perpetrators, not to recover victims' stolen funds, setting a clear expectation that a police report is unlikely to lead to financial restitution.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Goodman
insights.so_what: Victims of crypto theft should treat law enforcement engagement as pursuit of justice/deterrence, not as a fund-recovery mechanism, when deciding where to spend time and money post-hack.
insights.quote: Our job is to catch the bad guys. Our job is not to chase after your money.

insights.claim: No full class-action lawsuit against Coin Kite is expected because class actions require an outside litigation funder to see enough recoverable value to justify financing the suit, and Coin Kite is described as a roughly 10-person private Canadian company unlikely to hold anywhere near the $100M+ needed to cover total losses.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Goodman
insights.so_what: When evaluating recovery odds after a hack of a small private vendor, check the company's actual balance sheet/insurance capacity before assuming a class action will make victims whole — litigation economics, not moral responsibility, determine what gets pursued.
insights.quote: there's not going to be a class action lawsuit... Because in order for there to be a class action lawsuit, there needs to be enough money at play in order to pay for a class action lawsuits.

insights.claim: Instead of a class action, smaller law firms are forming targeted 'small group suits' of the highest-balance victims seeking settlements in the $10-15 million range, deliberately sized to avoid bankrupting Coin Kite (since a bankruptcy would leave nothing to recover) and to be among the first litigants to file.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Goodman
insights.so_what: Post-hack legal strategy for a thinly-capitalized defendant favors small, fast, targeted suits over large class actions — a pattern likely to repeat in future crypto-custody breaches involving small vendors.

insights.claim: In the small-group-suit structure being offered to him, victims (not the law firm) bear the financial risk by paying retainers proportional to their losses with no guarantee of recovery, and the firm is not offering even partial contingency — which the guest views as a signal the firm itself doubts a large recovery is likely.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Goodman
insights.so_what: A law firm's unwillingness to share downside risk on a contingency basis is itself useful diligence information about how confident insiders actually are in a claim's recovery prospects.
insights.quote: It's a bit of a tell, right? If they really believed that there was a lot of money to be had here, that it was as sure as they say it is, a law firm would say, you know, we'll take some of the risk for more of the upside.

insights.claim: Total losses from the Cold Card hack were cited at over $100 million at the time (with dollar-denominated losses rising further as Bitcoin's price has since increased), though this is still described as small relative to mega-hacks like FTX.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Goodman
insights.so_what: Frames the scale of the Cold Card incident within the broader history of crypto losses, useful context for sizing potential litigation, regulatory response, or industry reputational impact.

insights.claim: The guest maintains high conviction that Bitcoin's core investment thesis is unchanged by the hack because the failure originated in a specific hardware vendor's implementation, not in Bitcoin's protocol itself, and he plans to keep buying Bitcoin going forward.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Goodman
insights.so_what: Distinguishes protocol-level risk from vendor/implementation risk in the self-custody stack — a distinction investors should apply when a custody-related incident might otherwise be mistaken for a thesis-breaking event.
insights.quote: This was not a failure of Bitcoin. This is a failure of a hardware company.

insights.claim: Even as a strong believer in Bitcoin's asymmetric expected-value profile, the guest deliberately did not allocate all of his net worth to it, reasoning that avoiding catastrophic, game-ending risk matters more than maximizing upside on a bet that is already asymmetric by nature.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Goodman
insights.so_what: A practical position-sizing rule for any high-conviction asymmetric bet: size it so a worst-case, unforeseeable failure (hack, fraud, regulatory shock) cannot remove you from future opportunity, even if that means leaving some expected return on the table.
insights.quote: I can afford to not get stupid stinking rich. I can't afford to get taken out of the game.

insights.claim: The guest treats Bitcoin as one of four pillars in a broader personal investment system explicitly built to withstand unexpected catastrophic failure in any single pillar, rather than concentrating all conviction into one asset or vehicle.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Goodman
insights.so_what: Portfolio construction that assumes any single sleeve — including a high-conviction asymmetric bet — could go to zero from an unforeseen operational failure, not just market risk, is a resilience test worth applying broadly.

insights.claim: The guest maxed out his Canadian TFSA (a tax-advantaged account comparable to a Roth IRA) in QBTC, an early Bitcoin fund that predated U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs, back in 2020-2021, and still holds that position untouched even after the Cold Card hack.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Goodman
insights.so_what: Illustrates that regulated, custodial fund-wrapper exposure (QBTC/TFSA) was structurally insulated from a self-custody hardware failure, reinforcing custody-vehicle diversification as its own risk-reduction layer.

insights.claim: Despite losing all of his self-custodied Bitcoin (18+ BTC), the guest says he has not lost faith in self-custody as a concept and expects to hold Bitcoin directly again, but is not yet ready to decide whether he personally will return to self-custody given how recent the loss is.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Goodman
insights.so_what: Signals that high-profile custody failures can dampen individual appetite for self-custody without necessarily reducing appetite for the underlying asset — a distinction relevant to demand for custodial vs. self-custody products going forward.

insights.claim: The guest believes there is a good chance the hacker(s) will eventually be identified, citing Bitcoin's transparent, traceable public ledger as a structural advantage for investigators — drawing a parallel to how the Silk Road operator was eventually traced back through an old public forum post using his personal email years earlier — but believes there is a low chance victims will ever recover the stolen funds even if a perpetrator is caught.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Goodman
insights.so_what: Separates 'attacker gets caught' odds from 'funds get recovered' odds — investors should not assume a high-profile arrest implies restitution for victims.
insights.quote: how did the Silk Road guy get caught? like 5 years previous to when he built the website, he used his email account on some public forum.

insights.claim: Forensic trackers monitoring the stolen funds have reportedly observed very low liquidity when attackers attempt to run the Bitcoin through CoinJoin mixing services, which may still allow investigators to trace where the funds are moving.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Goodman
insights.so_what: Thin CoinJoin liquidity for large stolen sums is a practical constraint on laundering large hacked Bitcoin balances, which is a factor to watch for eventual on-chain attribution or fund freezes at exchanges.
insights.quote: with the coin joins, there's been very low liquidity. So, if someone if a hacker tries to use one of them, you can kind of tell where that Bitcoin's moving and and where it's going.

insights.claim: An unverified theory circulating after the hack suggests it could have been a coordinated effort against self-custody intended to push users toward institutional custody providers; the guest explicitly labels this pure speculation with no supporting evidence.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Goodman
insights.so_what: Even as unconfirmed speculation, a narrative blaming self-custody itself (rather than one vendor) is worth monitoring, since it could shift retail and institutional demand toward custodial Bitcoin products if it gains traction.
insights.quote: maybe this was a coordinated effort against self-custody by people who wanted to push institutional custody

insights.claim: In the wake of the hack, the Bitcoin community formed a dedicated 'Bitcoin Red Team' of researchers actively probing hardware wallets and codebases for similar undiscovered vulnerabilities, which the guest believes will materially improve security across the broader self-custody ecosystem.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Goodman
insights.so_what: Expect increased third-party security auditing to become a competitive differentiator and possibly a purchase criterion for hardware-wallet vendors following this incident.

insights.claim: The guest states that code auditing across the self-custody hardware space has increased to a level not previously seen, as a direct consequence of the Cold Card incident.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Goodman
insights.so_what: A single high-profile vendor failure can trigger industry-wide security hardening, which may reduce tail risk for self-custody users broadly even though it originated from one company's mistake.
insights.quote: I feel like now everything has been audited... to a level that it wasn't before.
